nameStory: The Delta-spotted Spiketail gets its name from the distinctive triangular (delta-shaped) yellow spots that decorate its dark abdomen. The 'spiketail' part comes from the female's prominent egg-laying tube, called an ovipositor, which projects like a sharp spike from the tip of her abdomen. This fearsome-looking 'spike' is actually a precision tool for drilling eggs into stream bottoms!
description: The Delta-spotted Spiketail is one of New England's largest and most impressive dragonflies, with a wingspan that can reach nearly 4 inches. These robust, dark-bodied hunters have bright yellow triangular spots running down their black abdomens like a string of warning signs. Males patrol territories along streams and rivers with powerful, direct flight, while females use their prominent 'spike' to deposit eggs in sandy or muddy stream bottoms. They're part of the spiketail family, known for being some of our most primitive and powerful dragonflies.

idTips.label: Triangular yellow spots
idTips.description: Look for bright yellow, perfectly triangular spots arranged in pairs down the dark abdomen - they look like tiny yield signs against the black background

idTips.label: Large size and robust build
idTips.description: One of our biggest dragonflies with a thick, sturdy body that feels substantial compared to the more delicate darners and skimmers

idTips.label: Bright green eyes
idTips.description: Large, emerald-green compound eyes that meet at the top of the head, giving them an almost jewel-like appearance in sunlight

idTips.label: Female's prominent ovipositor
idTips.description: Females have an unmistakable sword-like projection extending from the abdomen tip - it looks almost medieval and is longer than in most other dragonfly species

idTips.label: Patrol flight pattern
idTips.description: Males fly back and forth along the same stretch of stream in a steady, methodical pattern, unlike the more erratic flight of other dragonflies

habitat: Look for Delta-spotted Spiketails along clean, flowing streams and small rivers throughout New England's forested areas. They prefer streams with sandy or gravelly bottoms where females can easily drill their eggs, often in partially shaded areas under forest canopy. You'll rarely find them far from flowing water, and they favor streams with good water quality and minimal pollution.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May and early June. Look for freshly emerged individuals with shiny wings resting near streams as they mature.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity from June through August. Males actively patrol stream territories during warm afternoons, and females can be seen hovering over water to lay eggs.
seasonality.fall: Activity decreases significantly by September, with only occasional late individuals spotted into early October before cold weather ends their season.
seasonality.winter: Adults are completely absent. Eggs and larvae remain hidden in stream bottoms, developing slowly through the cold months until spring emergence.

funFact: Female Delta-spotted Spiketails are living jackhammers - they hover over streams and literally drill their eggs into sand and gravel using their spike-like ovipositor, sometimes penetrating several inches deep into the stream bottom while their wings beat furiously to maintain position!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other large, dark dragonflies like darners, but spiketails have distinctly different body proportions - they're stockier with shorter, broader abdomens. Memory trick: 'Spiketails are built like tanks, darners are built like rockets' - spiketails look robust and powerful, while darners appear sleek and streamlined.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their fearsome appearance and large size, spiketails are completely harmless to humans - that prominent 'spike' is only used for egg-laying and cannot sting or bite. The family name Cordulegastridae literally means 'club-belly' in reference to their robust abdominal shape.
compareHints: Delta-spotted Spiketails have more distinct, triangular yellow spots than the Twin-spotted Spiketail's paired round spots, and their spots are more numerous than the single large spots of Arrowhead Spiketails. Unlike the Tiger Spiketail's striped pattern, Delta-spotted have clean, separate triangular markings that don't connect across the abdomen.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Twin-spotted Spiketails are distinguished from Delta-spotted Spiketails by having two round spots per segment rather than triangular markings, and from Tiger Spiketails by their smaller size and less bold yellow stripes.

Among its spiketail relatives, the Arrowhead Spiketail is distinguished by those distinctive arrow-shaped abdominal spots - Delta-spotted Spiketails have triangular spots that don't point directionally, while Twin-spotted Spiketails have paired round spots rather than arrows.
